text:
17track turned its REST API into a fully paid product, and the owner's API key stopped working as a result. That is why the plugin gained a second authentication mode built on pyseventeentrack, which drives the private buyer API behind the 17track website using an ordinary account email and password.

The api_token path was NOT removed, purely because other users may still pay for API access. The consequence is that nobody working on this plugin can execute the api_token code path any more. Every change to it is verified by static review and by the mocked checks in tests/test_api_path.py against the published API contract, never by running it. Treat that path as untestable and be correspondingly strict: an unconfirmed or unexpected response must fail loudly rather than be interpreted optimistically. A silent no-op bug already occurred there once, where a carrier override appeared to succeed but did nothing.

list_packages and remove_package deliberately refuse to run in account mode (email and password), even though it was proven possible to implement them there. Do not 'fix' this without asking.

A live probe against the private buyer API confirmed both are achievable: listing works through GetTrackInfoList, which supports paging via pageInfo {Page, PerPage, TotalCount} and filtering by tracking number through the Item field; removal works through SetTrackArchived with param {TrackInfoIds: [FTrackInfoId]}, though that archives rather than truly deletes.

It was declined on scope, not feasibility. The owner asked for these two tools to be kept 'just for the api path' and stated twice that his only real requirement was accurate tracking with carrier disambiguation. Implementing them for account mode would add surface for features he had explicitly set aside.

They refuse explicitly rather than acting as no-ops because a no-op list returns an empty set, and the assistant then tells the user they have no packages tracked, which is a confident false statement. A no-op removal reports success while the package remains.

The owner has drawn a hard line on how far the unofficial account mode may go: authenticated calls to buyer.17track.net only, using the account's own email and password via the pyseventeentrack login.

Explicitly OFF LIMITS, do not implement and do not propose:
  - The anonymous widget endpoint https://t.17track.net/track/restapi, or any other endpoint that requires forging Origin/Referer headers to impersonate 17track's own embeddable tracker.
  - Anything that defeats a bot challenge: Cloudflare workarounds, browser-fingerprint impersonation libraries (cloudscraper, curl_cffi, tls_client and friends), or browser automation.

The reasoning is a distinction between two kinds of unofficial. Logging in with the user's credentials and calling the endpoint the site itself calls when that user is logged in is a fragility the owner has accepted and documented in the README. Impersonating an anonymous browser widget and solving challenges is a different bargain: markedly more fragile, and it risks getting the account or the IP blocked.

This came up while investigating whether full package event history is retrievable. An agent probing for it reached the widget endpoint with spoofed Origin/Referer headers and then started planning browser automation to get past Cloudflare. It was stopped before anything was implemented. If event history turns out to be reachable ONLY through that route, then event history is not a feature this plugin gets.

Full package event history is NOT retrievable from the authenticated 17track buyer API. Do not re-investigate this without new information.

Probed live on 2026-08-27 against a real UPS package. GetTrackInfoById, called as method 'GetTrackInfoById' with param {isa: false, tids: [FTrackInfoId]}, DOES work and returns Code 0 — but its Json is the identical package object that GetTrackInfoList already returns. Same 18 fields, and the only event data in either response is FLastEvent, a single JSON-encoded event: {a: timestamp, c: location, z: description, dd: {d, t, tz}}.

The complete field set observed on a package: FCompleteUpdate, FCreateTime, FFirstCarrier, FFirstCarrierOptions, FFirstCarrierSource, FFirstCountry, FIsArchived, FLastEvent, FPackageState, FRemark, FSecondCarrier, FSecondCarrierSource, FSecondCountry, FStartAndEndInterval, FTrackInfoId, FTrackNo, FTrackStateType, source, tag, totop. No event list under any name.

The multi-event history shown on the 17track website is rendered from the anonymous widget endpoint t.17track.net/track/restapi, which is off limits (see the scope-boundaries entry). So history is not a feature this plugin can have, and the single latest event is the ceiling for account mode.

Consequence: track_package's output shape, with one latest_event/location/timestamp rather than an event array, is a hard limit of the data source, not a design shortcut.

When a tracking number is newly added to the account, 17track populates the carrier immediately but takes MINUTES to actually fetch data from that carrier. Measured on a real UPS package: FCreateTime 09:10:44, FCompleteUpdate 09:16:36 — about six minutes.

During that window GetTrackInfoList returns the package with FFirstCarrier set (17track infers it from the tracking number prefix, e.g. 1Z means UPS) but FPackageState and FLastEvent absent. The original code formatted that straight through, producing a result with a real carrier and null status, location, latest_event and timestamp, and reported it as success. The assistant then told the user there were no events, which reads as 'this package has no tracking information' when the truth was '17track has not looked yet'. This is what prompted the pending-state work.

Six minutes cannot be waited out inside the tool's 30-second budget, so retrying harder is not an option — the tool has to report not-ready and let the user come back.

Note the distinction that the detection rule depends on: FPackageState ABSENT means not fetched yet, whereas FPackageState == 0 means 17track did fetch and the carrier genuinely has nothing ('Not Found'). Those must not be collapsed.
